entries.description: A bacterial disease that can affect tomato seedlings, foliage, and fruit. Similar leaf symptoms can have other causes, so image classification alone is not confirmation.
symptoms: Water-soaked areas on leaves that darken from yellow or light green to brown or black
Fruit spots may become brown and scabby
favorable_weather_conditions: High relative humidity and free moisture on plant surfaces
Symptoms develop rapidly at temperatures around 20 °C (68 °F) and above; cool nights may suppress development
prevention: Use pathogen-free seed and disease-free transplants where available
Avoid sprinkler irrigation where practical
Rotate with a nonhost crop
general_management: Avoid moving water from infected plants onto healthy plants
Use clean planting material and monitor plants
Seek local agricultural extension advice for diagnosis and locally appropriate management

sources.organization: UC Statewide IPM Program, University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
sources.title: UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines: Tomato — Bacterial Spot

entries.description: A fungal disease affecting tomato foliage, stems, and fruit, often first noticed on older lower foliage.
symptoms: Round brown leaf spots, often with concentric target-like rings
Yellowing around spots and premature leaf death may occur
Dark, leathery fruit spots can occur near the stem
favorable_weather_conditions: Moderate to warm temperatures, especially with wet foliage, heavy dew, or relative humidity around 90% or higher
prevention: Use disease-free planting material
Mulch soil to reduce splash
Water at the plant base and maintain airflow
Rotate away from tomato and related crops for at least two years where feasible
general_management: Scout lower foliage regularly
Remove affected leaves carefully and clean tools
Keep foliage dry where practical and obtain local extension guidance if symptoms progress

sources.title: Early blight in tomato and potato

entries.description: A fungal disease of potato and other solanaceous crops that commonly develops on older foliage and can affect stems and tubers/fruiting parts.
symptoms: Dark round leaf spots that may develop concentric rings
Yellowing and drying around lesions; older leaves are commonly affected first
favorable_weather_conditions: Moderate to warm temperatures combined with wet weather or heavy dew; high relative humidity favors spread
prevention: Maintain crop rotation and manage infected plant debris
Avoid overhead irrigation where practical
Support airflow and reduce soil splash
general_management: Scout older foliage and remove infected debris
Use disease-free planting material and seek locally appropriate extension advice

sources.title: Early blight in tomato and potato

entries.description: A rapidly spreading disease caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans that can affect tomato foliage, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Large dark brown leaf blotches with green-gray edges, not limited by major veins
White growth may appear on infected tissue in humid conditions
Firm dark brown fruit spots may enlarge
favorable_weather_conditions: Cool, damp conditions, commonly around 60–70 °F (16–21 °C); prolonged hot, dry weather can slow spread
prevention: Inspect transplants before planting
Keep foliage dry where practical and provide airflow
Avoid planting in recently used solanaceous-crop areas where feasible
general_management: Scout frequently; suspected late blight warrants prompt confirmation and consultation with local extension because it can spread rapidly
Remove confirmed infected plant material following local guidance
Use certified disease-free potato seed when planting potatoes

sources.title: Late blight of tomato and potato

entries.description: A rapidly spreading disease caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans affecting potato foliage and tubers.
symptoms: Large dark brown leaf blotches with green-gray edges
White growth may appear on infected tissue in humid conditions
Infected tubers may be discolored, shrunken, or develop soft rot
favorable_weather_conditions: Cool, damp conditions, commonly around 60–70 °F (16–21 °C); prolonged hot, dry weather can slow spread
prevention: Plant certified potato seed
Control volunteer potato plants and manage cull piles
Maintain airflow and avoid prolonged leaf wetness where practical
general_management: Scout frequently and promptly seek local extension guidance for suspected cases
Remove or manage infected plants and crop residues according to local guidance

entries.description: A destructive fungal disease of grapes caused by Guignardia bidwellii (anamorph Phyllosticta ampelicida) that attacks all green vine tissues including leaves, shoots, petioles, and developing fruit clusters.
symptoms: Small, circular to angular reddish-brown or tan spots on leaves with distinct dark borders
Tiny black specks (fungal fruiting bodies called pycnidia) embedded in leaf lesions, often arranged in a ring near the margin
Sunken, dark elongated cankers on young shoots, petioles, and cluster stems
Infected berries soften, turn brown, and rapidly shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies that often remain attached to cluster stems
favorable_weather_conditions: Warm temperatures (around 20–27 °C / 68–80 °F) combined with free moisture on foliage from rain or heavy dew
High relative humidity (80% or higher) that slows canopy drying and favors spore release and infection
prevention: Sanitation: collect and destroy mummified berries from the canopy and ground during dormant pruning to remove primary inoculum
Canopy management: prune and position shoots to promote rapid drying of foliage and cluster exposure to sunlight and airflow
Manage weeds and floor vegetation under the trellis to reduce ground humidity
general_management: Scout young leaves and shoot bases early in the growing season, especially from immediate pre-bloom through early fruit set
Prune out infected cane cankers during dormant pruning
Consult local university agricultural extension or viticulture advisors for regional disease timing and locally approved management options

sources.title: UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines: Grape

entries.description: A chronic grapevine trunk disease complex caused by wood-colonizing fungi (primarily Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium species) that infect the vascular wood of mature vines, producing foliar symptoms and berry spotting.
symptoms: Distinctive 'tiger-stripe' foliar symptoms with chlorotic and necrotic interveinal bands between green veins (stripes turn red on red cultivars and yellow on white cultivars before drying)
Severe hot-weather form (apoplexy) where shoots or entire vines wilt and dry up suddenly
Small, round, dark purple-to-black spots resembling measles on developing berries, which may crack or dry out
Dark vascular streaking and spongy wood decay visible in cross-sections of infected trunks or cordons
favorable_weather_conditions: Foliar and berry symptom expression is strongly aggravated by summer heat, high evaporative demand, and moisture stress following winter infection periods
prevention: Pruning wound protection: apply approved wound protectants or sealants to large pruning cuts, particularly during wet dormant seasons
Delay pruning until late in the dormant season when wounds heal more rapidly and spore flight may be lower
Plant certified disease-free nursery rootstock and scion wood
general_management: Mark symptomatic vines during the growing season when foliar tiger-striping and measles symptoms are most visible
Practice vine renewal or remedial surgery by retraining healthy basal suckers if trunk infection is localized above the graft union
Disinfect pruning shears between vines to minimize mechanical transmission
Consult regional viticulture extension specialists for trunk disease assessment and sustainable vineyard renewal strategies

sources.organization: UC Statewide IPM Program, University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
sources.title: UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines: Grape — Esca (Black Measles)

entries.description: A late-season foliar fungal disease of grapevines caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (historically classified as Isariopsis clavispora or Phaeoisariopsis clavispora; teleomorph Mycosphaerella personata) that primarily infects mature leaves.
symptoms: Large, irregular or angular dark reddish-brown to black spots on leaves, often partially delimited by leaf veins
Lesions become dry and brittle with age, sometimes dropping out
Dark velvety or olivaceous fungal growth (conidiophores) develops on the undersides of leaf spots in humid weather
Premature defoliation in severe or late-season infections, which can impede late fruit maturation and vine carbohydrate storage
favorable_weather_conditions: Persistent high relative humidity (85% or higher) and prolonged leaf surface wetness from rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew
Warm, humid late-summer conditions in dense canopies with restricted air movement
prevention: Canopy management: practice shoot thinning, suckering, and leaf removal around the fruiting zone to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration
Avoid overhead irrigation that wets the canopy and prolongs leaf surface wetness
Sanitation: manage fallen leaf debris after harvest to reduce overwintering fungal structures
general_management: Scout older, mature leaves in the interior and lower canopy during mid-to-late summer
Maintain balanced vine nutrition and avoid excessive vegetative growth that impedes airflow
Consult regional agricultural extension viticulture advisors for local disease risk evaluation and integrated canopy management
